activities.anchor: tools meet a live balance sheet
activities.caption: file the decisions: invest, fund, or return
activities.name: cfThreeBuckets

config.prompt: Every corporate-finance decision lands in one of three drawers — file them:

items.label: take the factory with NPV +16.2 or reject it
issue bonds or shares for the expansion
declare a dividend or repurchase shares
rank projects by profitability index under rationing
choose 7% rather than 10% as the hurdle
initiate a dividend to signal durable cash

config.why: The third drawer looks trivial and turns out to be a signalling game; the second carries the most famous 'it doesn't matter' result in all of social science.

activities.anchor: Watch how sensitive the answer is
activities.caption: steer the hurdle — watch the NPV profile flip
activities.name: cfNpvPlotter

curves.label: NPV of the project at hurdle rate x

activities.anchor: Three refinements cover almost all practical cases
activities.caption: spend the 1,000 — find the best combination
activities.name: cfRationBranch

config.root: The budget is 1,000. A needs 300 to return 450 (NPV 150, PI 1.5); B needs 500 to return 700 (NPV 200, PI 1.4); C needs 400 to return 560 (NPV 160, PI 1.4).

start.text: PI-ranking greedily takes A (300 spent), then B (800 spent). C costs 400 — over budget. What now?

choices.label: Settle for A + B
choices.feedback: Total NPV 350 — respectable, but one combination beats it.

choices.label: Swap B out for C: run A + C
choices.feedback: 310 — the swap costs more than it gains.

choices.label: Re-search the combinations from scratch
choices.feedback: With lumpy, indivisible projects, PI is a heuristic, not an optimizer — combinations must be searched.

combo.text: The search finds B + C: 900 spent, NPV 360 — beating A + B's 350 with 100 of budget left idle by choice, not by the ranking.

config.why: PI ranks efficiently but a lower-ranked pair can be worth more together — which is why the NPV rule, not payback, remains the referee.

activities.anchor: no way to choose between them
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the IRR briefing
activities.name: cfIrrSpot

config.prompt: One line of this project-briefing is wrong — click it:
lines: When projects compete, take the highest NPV, not the highest IRR.
A small kiosk can show a spectacular IRR and still add less value than a duller, larger factory.
IRR assumes each year's cash flows are reinvested at the honest, attainable discount rate.
When cash flows change sign more than once, IRR can produce two or more answers.
That is why mining projects — build, harvest, clean up — are the textbook IRR trap.
config.correction: IRR assumes reinvestment at the IRR itself — a spectacular IRR presumes spectacular reinvestment; only NPV assumes the honest, attainable discount rate.
config.why: NPV's reinvestment assumption is the attainable one, and a single sign change too many can mint multiple IRRs with no way to rank them.

activities.anchor: The hurdle rate comes from the funding mix
activities.caption: pair each input with its price
activities.name: cfCostMatch

config.prompt: Pricing the hurdle — pair each input with what it costs or claims:

pairs.right: contractually cheap — priority in bankruptcy, and interest is tax-deductible
the residual claim, paid last, demanding the most — priced with CAPM
(1 − t) applied to interest only; dividends are not deductible
weights from today's prices — a firm whose shares tripled still re-weights
the blend that turns the funding mix into the hurdle rate

config.why: The two classic slips — book-value weights and a tax shield on the wrong flow — are exactly what the worked example warns against.

activities.caption: call the ratchet — what equity demands at D/E = 2
activities.name: cfPropIIEstimate

config.prompt: Proposition II: with r_A = 10% and r_D = 6%, what return must equity holders demand at D/E = 2?
config.why: r_E = r_A + (D/E) × (r_A − r_D) = 10% + 2 × 4% = 18% — and the blend (1/3 × 18% + 2/3 × 6%) still averages 10%. Debt is cheaper per unit, but it makes every remaining unit of equity riskier and more expensive.
config.context: Check the blend: one-third at 18% plus two-thirds at 6% still averages exactly 10%.

activities.anchor: cash arrives later than it must leave
activities.caption: fill the cycle — where the cash sits
activities.name: cfCccCloze

config.text: The worked firm holds inventory %%0%% days (DIO), collects %%1%% days after sale (DSO) and pays suppliers after %%2%% days (DPO): cash is locked up for %%3%% days — on revenue of 7.3 million, roughly 1.3 million of permanent funding.
config.hint: DIO + DSO − DPO. Squeeze DSO to 30 and you release about 0.3 million — the CFO's cheapest financing.

activities.anchor: are, at fair prices, economically identical
activities.caption: drag the divider — dividend vs buyback
activities.name: cfPayoutCompare

config.prompt: The same 10 million returned, two instruments — drag the divider:

before.label: Dividend
before.text: The share drops to 90 on the ex-date and the holder keeps 90 plus 10 of cash — and a commitment: cutting one is read as distress, while initiating one says 'this cash stream is durable'.

after.label: Buyback
after.text: 100,000 shares retired at 100: 900,000 shares now own a 90 million firm — still worth 100 each. Flexible, often taxed as capital gains, and a signal that shares are cheap — or that positive-NPV projects have run out.

config.why: At fair prices the arithmetic is identical; the differences are institutional — commitment versus flexibility, income versus gains — which is why payout choices signal.
